name: Dal baati churma
hook: Rajasthan on a plate: baked wheat balls, ghee, dal and a sweet crumble.
what: Baati are hard, round wheat rolls baked over coals or in an oven. They come with spiced lentils (dal) and churma, a sweet crumble of wheat, ghee and jaggery or sugar.
howToEat: Crack the baati with your fingers, let them pour ghee on (or say 'kam ghee'), dunk in dal, and eat churma in between bites. Then nap.
vegNote: Fully vegetarian. Very rich in ghee; ask for less if you like.

spots.name: Chulha Rasoi
spots.note: Simple family dhaba below the fort. Baati baked over cow-dung coals, the old way.

spots.name: Thali Haveli
spots.note: Unlimited Rajasthani thali. Come hungry and leave rolling.

name: Pyaaz kachori
hook: Flaky, deep-fried pastry stuffed with spiced onion. Jaipur's morning ritual.
what: A round, crisp pastry filled with onions cooked with spices and a little fennel. Served hot with tangy tamarind and green chutneys.
howToEat: Break it open, pour chutney into the middle, eat while hot. One is a snack; two is breakfast.
vegNote: Vegetarian. Contains onion, so not for those who avoid it. Ask for 'mawa kachori' if you want a sweet one.

spots.name: Chaupar Kachori Thela
spots.note: Hot batches every few minutes. Eat standing, like everyone else.

spots.name: Kesariya Mithai Ghar
spots.note: Busy sweet shop with kachori in the morning and sweets all day.

name: Mirchi vada
hook: A big green chilli, stuffed with potato and fried in gram-flour batter.
what: Large, mild green chillies are stuffed with spiced potato, dipped in besan batter and deep-fried until crisp.
howToEat: Eat it hot with chutney. The chilli is usually mild, but bite the tip first to check.
vegNote: Vegetarian and usually vegan, but check if it's fried in ghee.

spots.name: Ram Niwas Garden Pakode
spots.note: A cart near Albert Hall. Perfect while waiting for the lights to come on.

name: Ghewar
bestTimeLabel: After lunch or an evening treat
hook: A lacy, honeycomb disc of fried batter, soaked in syrup. Festive and messy.
what: Batter is poured into hot ghee to make a crisp, web-like disc, then soaked in sugar syrup and often topped with sweetened cream (malai) and nuts.
howToEat: Break a piece with your fingers or a spoon. Malai ghewar is richer; plain is crunchier. Share one; it's big.
vegNote: Vegetarian. Made with ghee and milk, so not vegan. Most special around the monsoon festivals of Teej and Raksha Bandhan, but many sweet shops sell it year-round.

spots.name: Mithaas Bhandar
spots.note: Old-style sweet shop near the palace. Ask for a small piece to taste first.

spots.name: Gulabi Mishthan
spots.note: Packs ghewar in boxes that survive a flight, mostly.

name: Laal maas
hook: Fiery red mutton curry, slow-cooked with Mathania chillies. Not for the faint-hearted.
what: Mutton slow-cooked with yoghurt, garlic and plenty of red chillies, which give the deep red colour. A classic dish of Rajput kitchens.
howToEat: Tear bajra roti or plain roti and scoop. Keep a glass of chaas or lassi nearby. You'll need it.
vegNote: Non-vegetarian (mutton). Vegetarians: try gatte ki sabzi or ker sangri instead.

spots.name: Mehfil-e-Rasoi
spots.note: Ask for 'thoda kam teekha' if you're new to it; they won't judge. Much.

spots.name: Qila Dhaba
spots.note: Rough-and-ready dhaba on the Amer road. Generous portions.

name: Gatte ki sabzi
hook: Gram-flour dumplings in a tangy yoghurt curry. Desert cooking at its smartest.
what: Dough made from besan (gram flour) and spices is rolled, boiled, sliced and simmered in a spiced yoghurt gravy. Made for a land where fresh vegetables were scarce.
howToEat: With roti or rice. It's a staple of every Rajasthani thali, so you'll likely meet it there first.

spots.name: Gaon Ki Rasoi
spots.note: Homely lunch stop after the printing workshops.

spots.name: Pink Thali House
spots.note: Good-value thali with gatte, kadhi and bajra roti.

name: Lassi
hook: Thick, cold, sweet yoghurt in a clay kulhad, topped with malai.
what: Yoghurt churned with sugar (or salt) and sometimes saffron or cardamom, served thick in a kulhad, a little clay cup.
howToEat: Use the spoon for the malai on top first, then drink. Ask for 'meethi' (sweet) or 'namkeen' (salty).
vegNote: Vegetarian; contains dairy. If your stomach is new to India, choose busy shops with fresh batches.

spots.name: Malai Kulhad Corner
spots.note: Thick enough to stand a spoon in. Sells out by late afternoon.

spots.name: Chaupar Lassi Bhandar
spots.note: A handy stop after Jantar Mantar.

name: Masala chai
hook: Milky, sweet tea boiled with ginger and cardamom. Jaipur runs on it.
what: Black tea boiled with milk, sugar and spices like ginger, cardamom and sometimes clove or black pepper. Served in small glasses or kulhads.
howToEat: Sip it hot from the little glass. Pair with a kachori or a biscuit. Say 'cheeni kam' for less sugar.
vegNote: Vegetarian; contains milk. Some stalls can make it without sugar if you ask.

spots.name: Nahargarh Road Tapri
spots.note: Last chai stop before the climb to Nahargarh.

spots.name: Amer Ghati Chai
spots.note: Early-morning chai near the stepwell. The ginger is serious.
